questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.syllabus_ref: Unit 5: 5.2 Operations methods (flow production and the capacity of a line of dependent stages), with 3.3 Costs and revenues and 5.1 The role of operations management
questions.subtopic: 5.2 The output of a flow line is set by its slowest stage, so adding capacity anywhere else produces nothing, and the choice between buying capacity at the bottleneck and buying overtime at the bottleneck is a choice between a fixed cost and a variable one

stimulus.title: A four-stage flow line
stimulus.body: A manufacturer makes a single product on a flow line of four stages, in the order cutting, welding, assembly and finishing. Each stage is worked by one machine, and the product passes through all four stages in that order. Each machine is available for 2 400 minutes in a working week. The table gives the time each stage takes to process one unit. The machines are not shared, so a machine that is idle at one stage cannot be used to relieve a stage that is behind. Demand is steady at 600 units a week and the manufacturer is currently unable to meet it, which is costing sales.

table.caption: Processing time at each stage, in minutes per unit

questions.challenge_mechanism: The item is built on a single idea that is easy to state and easy to forget while computing: the output of a line of dependent stages is set by the slowest stage, so capacity added anywhere else changes nothing. The arithmetic is simple enough that a candidate can compute the capacity of all four stages, identify the welding stage as the bottleneck and still answer the third part by adding the second machine at the assembly stage and reporting a rise in output, because the candidate has computed the new capacity of assembly and looked at that number rather than at the line. The third and fourth parts are the same calculation applied to two different stages and they have opposite answers, which is the whole of the item. The final part then asks the candidate to compare a fixed cost with a variable one, where the weekly figures are close enough that the answer depends on the horizon and on how much flexibility the manufacturer values.
questions.question: The manufacturer's four-stage line has one machine at each stage, and each machine is available for 2 400 minutes a week. The times per unit are given in the table. Demand is steady at 600 units a week and the manufacturer cannot meet it, so it is losing sales that it could otherwise make. The operations manager has two proposals. The first is to buy a second welding machine at a cost of 85 000 dollars, which would halve the time the welding stage takes per unit, and which would be depreciated over five years. The second is to work overtime at whichever stage is limiting output, at an overtime rate of 36 dollars an hour, which is available whenever it is needed and can be stopped at any time. The operations manager has also considered buying a second assembly machine and has asked what difference that would make, since assembly takes four minutes a unit and is the stage the manager believed to be the problem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the weekly capacity of each of the four stages, and state which stage has the smallest capacity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the maximum number of units the line can produce in a week at present, and the shortfall against the weekly demand of 600 units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the effect on the line's weekly output of installing a second assembly machine, showing the capacity of every stage after the change.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the effect on the line's weekly output of installing a second welding machine, and explain why the two answers in (c) and (d) differ.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Evaluate whether the manufacturer should buy the welding machine or pay for overtime, using the weekly costs of each and considering the manufacturer's circumstances.

questions.answer:
(a) The weekly capacity of a stage is the minutes available divided by the minutes each unit takes at that stage. With 2 400 minutes available at every stage:

Cutting: 2 400 / 3.0 = 800 units a week.
Welding: 2 400 / 5.0 = 480 units a week.
Assembly: 2 400 / 4.0 = 600 units a week.
Finishing: 2 400 / 2.5 = 960 units a week.

The welding stage has the smallest capacity, at 480 units a week.

(b) A unit must pass through all four stages, so the line can produce no more units in a week than its slowest stage can pass. Welding is the slowest stage at 480 units a week, so the maximum weekly output is 480 units. Demand is 600 units a week, so the shortfall is 600 - 480 = 120 units a week, and those 120 units of sales are lost every week.

The other stages are not working at their limit. At an output of 480 units a week, cutting is using 480 x 3.0 = 1 440 of its 2 400 minutes, which is sixty per cent of its capacity; assembly is using 480 x 4.0 = 1 920 minutes, which is eighty per cent; and finishing is using 480 x 2.5 = 1 200 minutes, which is fifty per cent. Welding is using all 2 400 minutes, which is one hundred per cent.

(c) A second assembly machine halves the time assembly takes per unit, from 4.0 minutes to 2.0 minutes, so the capacity of assembly becomes 2 400 / 2.0 = 1 200 units a week. The capacities of the four stages are then 800 at cutting, 480 at welding, 1 200 at assembly and 960 at finishing.

The slowest stage is still welding, at 480 units a week, so the output of the line does not change. It remains 480 units a week and the shortfall remains 120 units a week. The money spent on the second assembly machine buys no additional output at all, because assembly was not limiting the line; the 120 extra units a week that the second machine could pass through cannot reach it, since welding cannot send them on.

(d) A second welding machine halves the time welding takes per unit, from 5.0 minutes to 2.5 minutes, so the capacity of welding becomes 2 400 / 2.5 = 960 units a week. The capacities of the four stages are then 800 at cutting, 960 at welding, 600 at assembly and 960 at finishing.

The slowest stage is now assembly, at 600 units a week, so the output of the line rises to 600 units a week, which is exactly the demand. The shortfall is closed. Welding is no longer the constraint and has spare capacity of 360 units a week; cutting is now the next tightest stage after assembly, at 800 units a week.

The two answers differ because output is governed by the slowest stage and by nothing else. In (c) the stage that was improved was not the slowest stage, so the line's output was still set by welding and did not move. In (d) the stage that was improved was the slowest stage, so the constraint moved to assembly and the output rose until it reached the new limit. Improving a stage that is not the constraint does not raise output; it only adds idle capacity to a stage that already had some. This is why the operations manager's belief that assembly was the problem was mistaken: assembly takes four minutes a unit, which is longer than cutting and longer than finishing, but welding takes five, and it is the longest time per unit that sets the pace.

(e) Either route closes the 120-unit shortfall, and the choice turns on the shape of the cost rather than on the size of it.

Overtime at the welding stage costs 36 dollars an hour. To make 120 extra units at 5.0 minutes a unit requires 120 x 5.0 = 600 minutes, which is 10 hours a week. At 36 dollars an hour that is 360 dollars a week, or 18 720 dollars a year. Overtime is a variable cost: it is paid only when the extra output is wanted, and it can be stopped in a week in which demand falls.

The welding machine costs 85 000 dollars depreciated over five years, which is 17 000 dollars a year, or about 326.92 dollars a week. It is a fixed cost: it is incurred every week whether the extra 120 units are made or not, and it commits the manufacturer for five years.

On cost alone the machine is slightly cheaper, at about 326.92 dollars a week against 360 dollars a week, which is about 2.72 dollars per extra unit against 3.00 dollars. Over five years the saving is roughly 1 720 dollars a year, about 8 600 dollars in total, which is small against an outlay of 85 000 dollars, and the payback on the machine is very long if it is justified only by the shortfall. The machine does have advantages beyond the weekly cost. It raises welding capacity to 960 units a week, so it leaves room for demand to grow to 600 units without any further spending, whereas overtime has to be paid for every extra unit and becomes more expensive if demand rises. It also removes the dependence on staff being willing to work overtime week after week, which is difficult to sustain and which raises the risk of absence and of poor quality on a tired shift.

Against that, the machine is a commitment. If demand falls, the 85 000 dollars is spent and the depreciation continues, while overtime can be cancelled. The manufacturer's position is not stated in the case, and the recommendation has to turn on it.

On the information given, the manufacturer should pay the overtime in the first instance, and revisit the machine if demand rises or proves to be permanent. The shortfall is 120 units a week, which is twenty per cent of demand, and the cost difference between the two routes is small enough, about 33 dollars a week, that it does not by itself justify an 85 000-dollar commitment. Overtime keeps the manufacturer flexible while it establishes whether the extra demand is durable, and it can be replaced by the machine once the demand has been shown to be permanent. The machine becomes the better choice as soon as demand is expected to rise towards the new welding capacity of 960 units, or as soon as the overtime proves difficult to staff; at that point the fixed cost is being spread over a larger output and the flexibility that overtime buys is no longer worth its price.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) One mark for the correct method, minutes available divided by minutes per unit, one mark for the four capacities 800, 480, 600 and 960, and one mark for identifying welding as the smallest. Follow-through is allowed from one arithmetic slip if the identification is consistent with the candidate's own figures.

(b) One mark for the output of 480 units a week, one mark for the shortfall of 120, and one mark for the reason, that output is limited by the slowest stage. A candidate who adds the stage capacities or takes the average has not understood the line and scores zero for this part.

(c) One mark for the new assembly capacity of 1 200 units a week, one mark for the statement that output is unchanged at 480 units a week, and one mark for the reason, that welding is still the slowest stage. An answer that reports a rise in output because assembly capacity has risen scores zero for this part, however correct the arithmetic.

(d) One mark for the new welding capacity of 960 units a week, one mark for the new output of 600 units a week with assembly as the new constraint, and one mark for the explanation that improving the constraint moves the constraint while improving any other stage changes nothing. Accept 600 units as the output because it matches demand; a candidate who states that assembly now limits the line at 600 units a week has the point even if the answer is expressed as 'up to 600'.

(e) No mark for naming a route. One mark for the correct weekly costs, overtime at 360 dollars a week or 18 720 dollars a year and the machine at about 326.92 dollars a week or 17 000 dollars a year, one mark for identifying the machine as the fixed cost and overtime as the variable one and drawing the consequence for flexibility, and one mark for a recommendation that states what would change it. A candidate who recommends the machine because it is cheaper per week takes two marks only if the flexibility argument is also addressed; the cost difference alone, at about 33 dollars a week, does not settle the question.
questions.explanation:
The theory of constraints is one of the few ideas in operations management that is both simple and counter-intuitive, and this item is arranged so that the counter-intuitive part cannot be avoided. The line has four stages, the times per unit are given, and the capacities follow by division. Nothing about the first two parts is hard. The third part then spends money on the stage the operations manager believes to be the problem, and the correct answer is that the spending achieves nothing.

That answer is available only to a candidate who has understood that output is set by the slowest stage. A candidate who has learned the calculation but not the idea will compute the new capacity of assembly, see that it has risen from 600 to 1 200 units a week, and report that output has risen. The item is designed so that this error produces a plausible, internally consistent and entirely wrong answer, which is why parts (c) and (d) are the same calculation applied to two stages and are marked separately. A candidate who gets (c) wrong will usually get (d) right, since improving the bottleneck obviously helps, and the pair together therefore separates understanding from procedure.

The last part moves from the physical constraint to the commercial one. Both routes close the shortfall, and the weekly costs are close: about 326.92 dollars for the machine against 360 dollars for the overtime. A candidate who decides on the weekly cost alone will choose the machine and will be able to justify it, but the justification is thin, because the difference is about 33 dollars a week against a commitment of 85 000 dollars. The interesting question is which cost is fixed and which is variable, and the case gives no information about how durable the demand is, so the honest answer is conditional: buy the flexibility first and the capacity later, unless the demand is known to be permanent. The item rewards that conditionality, and it rewards the candidate who notices that the machine also raises welding capacity beyond demand and therefore has value that the overtime route does not.

provenance.adaptation: Original. Flow production, capacity and the identification of a bottleneck are standard content in every operations management course, and the arithmetic of capacity from time per unit is routine. What is constructed here is the shape of the question: the manager proposes spending on a stage that is not the constraint, so that the correct answer to the third part is that nothing changes, and the same calculation is then applied to the constraint so that the two answers can be contrasted directly. The final part sets a fixed cost against a variable cost whose weekly figures are close, so that the recommendation turns on flexibility and on the durability of demand rather than on the arithmetic. The four stages, the times, the demand, the prices and the machine cost are original, and every capacity, utilisation and cost was computed and checked programmatically.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Compute the capacity of each of the four stages, identify the smallest, and then treat each stage's capacity as though it were independently useful, so that raising the capacity of any stage is expected to raise the output of the line in proportion to the capacity that has been added.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The output of the line is not the sum of the stages' capacities nor their average but the capacity of the slowest stage, so only the constraint has any effect on output and the capacity added anywhere else is absorbed as idle time, which is why the same kind of spending produces a rise in output at one stage and no change at all at another.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The second assembly machine is reported as raising weekly output, because assembly's capacity rises from 600 to 1 200 units a week and the candidate reads the new capacity as the new output; the shortfall against demand is then said to be closed, although welding still passes only 480 units a week and the line's output is unchanged.

verification.method: Every capacity was computed as the minutes available divided by the minutes per unit, and the line's output was taken as the smallest of the four rather than as any combination of them. The utilisation of each stage at the constrained output was computed to confirm that welding is at one hundred per cent while the others are not, which is the check that welding is genuinely the constraint. Each proposed change was then re-evaluated by recomputing all four capacities and taking the new smallest, and the two cases were confirmed to differ: the assembly change leaves the smallest at 480 while the welding change raises it to 600. The overtime hours were computed from the extra units and the bottleneck time, the overtime cost was annualised over fifty-two weeks, and the machine was annualised over its five-year life; the two routes were then compared per week and per extra unit.
solution_skeleton: divide the minutes available by the minutes per unit to get each stage's capacity
take the smallest capacity as the output of the line and subtract demand from it
recompute all four capacities after halving the assembly time and take the new smallest
recompute all four capacities after halving the welding time and take the new smallest
convert the extra units into overtime hours and into a weekly and annual cost
annualise the machine cost and compare the fixed and variable routes per week
